unit-hist-5ws.title: History · The 5 Ws and Reliable News
unit-hist-5ws.srcName: History — 5 Ws: Reliable vs Unreliable News (Drive)

summary.text: From the History extra-practice sheet: the five questions a news report should answer — Who, What, When, Where and Why — and how to judge whether a report can be trusted, using the author, the date, the source it came from, and whether the claim itself is believable.

why.text: Almost everything you will read online is written by someone who wants something. Knowing the four quick checks — who wrote it, when, where it was published, and is the claim reasonable — is one of the most useful habits there is, and it takes about ten seconds.

objectives.text: Answer all five Ws about a short news article
Judge a report as reliable or unreliable and give a reason
Notice when one of the five Ws is missing instead of guessing it
Explain why a named author and a date make a report checkable

parentNote.text: Built from the 5 Ws extra-practice sheet in the History folder. It uses the sheet's own two test headlines — the alien story and the kitten rescue — because the contrast between them is the whole lesson. Two ideas go slightly beyond the sheet and are worth talking about: a MISSING W should be named rather than guessed at, and when two sources both look plausible, the next move is checking whether other known outlets report the same thing.

nextUp.text: Cards first, then the quiz. Try the four checks on something you read this week.

cards.def:
**Who, What, When, Where and Why — the five questions a news report should answer.**
• Answer all five and you have understood the story.
• A report that leaves one out has a hole in it, and the hole is worth noticing.

**The people the story is about.**
• In a story about a new playground: the families who came, and the mayor who spoke.
• Not the reporter — the reporter wrote it, the Who is in it.

**The thing that happened.**
• "A brand-new playground opened." One sentence, no extra detail.
• Say it plainly first; the details belong to the other four questions.

**The time it happened.**
• "This Saturday." A date or a day, taken from the article rather than guessed.
• If the article never says, that is worth noticing too.

**The place it happened.**
• "Lincoln Park." As exact as the article makes it.

**The reason the story is worth reporting at all.**
• Kids in the area now have a safe place to play.
• This is the only one of the five that asks you to think rather than to find.
cards.hint: Four of the five you FIND in the article. Why-it-matters you WORK OUT.

cards.def:
**A report you have good reason to trust.**
• It names a real author, gives a date, and comes from a known news organisation.
• Reliable does not mean boring — it means checkable.

**A report you have good reason to doubt.**
• No author name, no date, an odd website, or a claim too wild to believe.
• One warning sign is enough to slow down; several together is a clear answer.

**The person who wrote it, named so you can check them.**
• "Written by Jane Martin" can be looked up. "Anonymous" cannot.
• Hiding the author is a choice, and it is worth asking why.

**When it was published.**
• A dated report can be checked against what else was happening.
• No date means you cannot tell whether it is news or years old.

**Who published it — the newspaper, station or website behind the report.**
• "City News Daily" is a news organisation. "spacefunnews.biz" says fun right in the name.
• Read the web address as part of the evidence.
cards.hint: The name of the website is a clue. Read it like you would read a headline.

opts: Who, What, When, Where and Why
Who, What, Where, Which and Why
What, When, Where, Whether and Why
Who, What, When, Why and How
questions.hint: Five questions, all starting with W.
steps: The five questions are Who, What, When, Where and Why.
Each one asks for a different piece of the story.
Answer all five and you have understood the report.

ex.main: **Who, What, When, Where and Why.** Five questions, and a full report answers all of them.
ex.tip: Say them in order every time. The habit is what makes you notice when one is missing.

questions.q: "A brand-new playground opened this Saturday at Lincoln Park." Which W does "at Lincoln Park" answer?
opts: Where
When
What
Who
steps: Where asks for the place something happened.
"At Lincoln Park" names the place.
"This Saturday" would answer When, and the playground opening is the What.

ex.tip: Match each phrase in a sentence to its W. One sentence often answers two or three at once.

questions.q: Which of these makes a news report MORE reliable?
opts: It names the author and gives a date
It has an exciting headline
It is very short
It appears on a colourful website
questions.hint: Which one can you actually check?
steps: A reliable report gives you things you can check.
An author with a name can be looked up; a date can be compared with other reports.
Excitement, length and colour tell you nothing about whether it is true.

ex.main: **Naming the author and the date.** Reliability is about what can be checked, not about how it looks.
ex.tip: Ask "could I check this?" Excitement is not evidence.

questions.q: Which of the 5 Ws asks you to think rather than just find the answer in the article?
opts: Why it matters
Who
When
Where
questions.hint: Four are hiding in the text. One is not.
steps: Who, What, When and Where are all stated somewhere in a good article.
Why it matters usually is not stated — you work it out from what happened.
That is what makes it the hardest of the five, and the most interesting.

ex.main: **Why it matters.** The other four you find; this one you work out.
ex.tip: If a question can be answered by pointing at a line, it is a finding question. If not, it needs your thinking.

questions.q: An article says: "Mayor Thompson said, 'We're happy to give kids a safe place to play.'" Who is the article about?
opts: The families and children using the new playground, and the mayor who opened it
Only Mayor Thompson
The reporter who wrote the article
The city workers who were paid for the project
questions.hint: Who is the story ABOUT, not who is quoted in it.
steps: Who asks about the people the story concerns.
The story concerns the families and children who gathered to use the playground.
The mayor appears too, as the person who opened it and spoke.
A reporter writes the story but is not in it.

ex.main: **The families and children, plus the mayor.** A quote makes someone part of the story, not the whole of it.
ex.tip: Careful with Who: the loudest voice in an article is not always what the article is about.

questions.q: Article A: "Aliens Land on School Roof and Eat Lunch in Cafeteria!" — Anonymous, no date, from www.spacefunnews.biz. Is it reliable?
opts: No — no author, no date, a joke website, and an unbelievable claim
Yes — it gives a specific location, so it can be checked
Yes — the headline is very detailed
It cannot be judged without reading the whole article
steps: No author is named, so nobody can be checked.
There is no date, so you cannot tell when or whether it happened.
The web address says "spacefunnews" — fun, not news.
And the claim itself is extraordinary. Four warning signs together is a clear answer.

ex.main: **No — four warning signs at once.** No author, no date, a joke source, and a wild claim.
ex.tip: One warning sign means slow down. Several together means you already have your answer.

questions.q: Article B: "Local Firefighters Rescue Kitten From Tree" — Jane Martin, August 4 2025, City News Daily. Is it reliable?
opts: Yes — a named author, a date, a real news source, and an ordinary claim
No — a kitten in a tree is too small to be real news
No — one newspaper is not enough to prove anything
Only if another newspaper reports the same thing
questions.hint: Check the same four things you used on the alien story.
steps: The author is named: Jane Martin, someone who can be looked up.
The date is given: August 4, 2025.
City News Daily is a news organisation, not a joke site.
And the event is ordinary — nothing about it demands extra proof.

ex.main: **Yes — it passes all four checks.** Named author, clear date, real source, believable claim.
ex.tip: Small stories can be perfectly reliable. Importance and reliability are different questions.

questions.q: A report answers Who, What, Where and Why, but never says when it happened. What should you do?
opts: Notice the gap and treat the report as incomplete until you find the date
Assume it happened today
Decide the whole report is false
Ignore it — four out of five is close enough
questions.hint: A missing W is information too.
steps: A complete report answers all five questions.
A missing When means you cannot tell whether this is news or years old.
That does not make it false — but it does make it incomplete, and worth checking.
Assuming a date would be inventing information, which is worse than noticing it is absent.

ex.main: **Notice the gap and go looking.** Missing is not the same as false, but it is worth knowing.
ex.tip: Never fill a missing W with a guess. Say "the article does not say" — that is the honest answer.

questions.q: Two websites report the same fire. One is "City News Daily", the other "realtruthnews.fun". Both name an author and a date. What should you check next?
opts: Whether other known news sources report the same thing
Which headline is more exciting
Which website loads faster
Which article is longer
questions.hint: They pass the same first checks. What separates them?
steps: Both have an author and a date, so those checks do not separate them.
The web addresses differ in character, but a name alone is not proof either way.
The strongest next step is to see whether other established news sources report the same event.
Agreement across independent sources is much harder to fake than one convincing-looking page.

ex.main: **Check whether other known sources report it too.** Independent agreement is the strongest signal you can get.
ex.tip: When the easy checks tie, look for a second source. One report is a claim; several independent ones are evidence.

questions.q: Why does a reliable news report name its author instead of publishing anonymously?
opts: So readers can check who wrote it and hold them responsible for getting it right
So the article looks longer
Because it is a legal requirement everywhere
So the newspaper can charge more for it
questions.hint: What can you do with a name that you cannot do without one?
steps: A named author can be looked up — what else they have written, and whether it held up.
It also means someone has put their reputation behind the report.
Anonymity removes both: nobody to check, and nobody answerable if it is wrong.
That is why "Anonymous" is a warning sign rather than a neutral detail.

ex.main: **So readers can check them and they are answerable for getting it right.** A name is accountability.
ex.tip: Ask what a detail lets you DO. A name lets you check and hold responsible; that is why it matters.

questions.q: What does the "What" question ask for?
opts: The thing that happened
The people involved
The reason it matters
The place it happened
questions.hint: Say the event plainly, in one sentence.
steps: What asks for the event itself.
"A brand-new playground opened" is the What.
People are the Who, the reason is the Why, the place is the Where.

ex.main: **The thing that happened.** Say it in one plain sentence and save the details for the other questions.
ex.tip: Answer What first. Once the event is clear, the other four fall into place around it.

questions.q: A website address ends in ".biz" and includes the word "fun". Why is that worth noticing?
opts: The name is a clue about what the site is for
Only .com websites are ever real
Long addresses are always false
It means the site is new
questions.hint: Read the address like a headline.
steps: A web address often says something about the publisher.
"spacefunnews.biz" puts fun in the middle of its own name.
That is a clue, not a proof — but it is worth reading before you trust the page.
Plenty of trustworthy sites use unusual endings, so it is one signal among several.

ex.main: **The name is a clue about what the site is for.** One signal, read alongside the author, the date and the claim.
ex.tip: No single check settles it. Stack them: author, date, source, and is the claim believable.

questions.q: A friend shows you a headline with no author and no date, but it says something you already believe. What should you do?
opts: Apply the same checks you would to anything else
Trust it, because it matches what you know
Reject it immediately for having no author
Share it and let others decide
questions.hint: Does agreeing with a story make it better evidence?
steps: The checks do not change based on whether you like the answer.
Agreeing with a claim is not evidence that it is true.
A missing author and date are still missing, so the report is still unchecked.
That does not make it false either — it means it needs checking, exactly like any other story.

ex.main: **Apply the same checks.** A story agreeing with you deserves the same scrutiny, not less.
ex.tip: The hardest source to question is the one you already agree with. That is exactly when to slow down.

questions.q: An article about the playground never explains why the story matters. How would you answer that W?
opts: Work it out: children in the area now have a safe place to play
Write "the article does not say" and stop
Copy the headline as the answer
Say the story does not matter at all
questions.hint: Why-it-matters is the one you work out rather than find.
steps: Four of the five Ws are found in the text; Why it matters usually is not.
You reason from what happened: a new playground was built for local families.
So the significance is that children in the area now have somewhere safe to play.
That reasoning is the answer — unlike a missing date, this W is meant to be worked out.

ex.main: **Work it out from what happened.** This is the one W you supply rather than find.
ex.tip: A missing DATE you report as missing. A missing WHY you reason your way to. Know which is which.

questions.q: Both a reliable and an unreliable article can have an exciting headline. What does that tell you about using headlines to judge a source?
opts: Headlines are written to attract readers, so they say little about reliability
Exciting headlines always mean a story is false
Dull headlines are always more reliable
Headlines are the best single test of a source
questions.hint: What is a headline actually FOR?
steps: A headline exists to make you want to read the article.
Both careful reporters and careless ones want readers, so both write attention-grabbing headlines.
Because it does not separate the two, a headline is weak evidence about reliability.
The author, the date and the publisher are far more useful, because they can be checked.

ex.main: **Headlines are built to attract readers, so they barely help.** Judge by what can be checked instead.
ex.tip: When a signal appears equally in true and false reports, it cannot tell them apart. Find a signal that can.
